title: Yogurt for a Hangover: Does It Help? The Probiotic Angle, Explained
excerpt: Is yogurt good for a hangover? What yogurt's protein, potassium, and probiotics can and can't do, Greek vs regular, kefir and ayran, and how to build a better hangover bowl.
metaDescription: Is yogurt good for a hangover? What its protein, potassium, and probiotics can and can't do, Greek vs regular yogurt, kefir, and the best bowl to make.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yogurt is a good food to eat with a hangover, but not because it fixes anything. It's cool, soft, and easy to get down when your stomach is unsettled. It gives you protein, some potassium, calcium, and a bit of fluid, and plain yogurt has much less sugar than most "hangover breakfasts." What yogurt does **not** do is clear alcohol, undo dehydration, or repair your gut overnight. There is no good evidence that the live cultures in yogurt make a hangover shorter or milder. Think of it as one of the gentlest, most useful foods to reach for, not as a remedy.

**The quick rules:** Pick plain yogurt (regular or Greek) with "live and active cultures" on the label. Eat a modest bowl, around three-quarters to one cup, and add something with carbs such as a banana, honey, or oats so your blood sugar gets a lift too. Drink water or an electrolyte drink alongside it, because yogurt alone won't rehydrate you. If dairy normally upsets your stomach, Greek yogurt or kefir is usually easier, and if you're vomiting, wait until you can keep sips of water down before trying food.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover after a night out gets better through the day. **Get medical help if** you can't keep any fluids down for many hours, you're vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, you have severe or worsening belly pain, black or bloody stools, signs of serious dehydration (very little urine, dizziness when you stand, a racing heart), confusion, or a high fever. If you drink most days and get shaking, sweating, anxiety, or seeing things when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous: talk to a doctor rather than waiting it out. If someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, or having a seizure, call 911.

## Is Yogurt Good for a Hangover?

Yes, in a modest, practical way. A hangover is a mix of things happening at once: poor sleep, mild dehydration, an irritated stomach, low-grade inflammation, sometimes low blood sugar, and the after-effects of acetaldehyde, the toxic by-product your liver makes when it breaks down alcohol. No single food addresses all of that. Yogurt helps with a few of the pieces:

- **It's easy on a queasy stomach.** It's cold, smooth, and mild. You don't have to chew it much, and it doesn't smell strongly, which matters when cooking smells make you feel worse.
- **It brings protein.** Protein helps you feel steadier and fuller than toast or juice alone, and it slows how quickly sugar from the rest of the meal hits your blood.
- **It has potassium and calcium.** Dairy foods are a decent source of potassium, one of the minerals you lose when alcohol makes you urinate more.
- **It contains water.** Yogurt is mostly water by weight, so it adds a little to your fluid intake, although not nearly enough on its own.
- **Plain yogurt is low in added sugar.** That's a real advantage over pastries, sugary cereals, or a large glass of juice, which can leave you crashing an hour later.

Where yogurt falls short is everything else. It doesn't speed up how fast your liver processes alcohol, it doesn't clear acetaldehyde in any meaningful way, and it won't fix the sleep you lost. The thing that actually ends a hangover is time.

## What's Actually in Yogurt (and Why It Matters the Morning After)

Exact numbers vary by brand and fat level, so treat these as rough ranges for a typical one-cup (about 245 g) serving of plain yogurt. Check your own label for specifics.

| Nutrient | Regular plain yogurt | Plain Greek yogurt | Why it matters after drinking |
|---|---|---|---|
| Protein | Around 9 to 13 g | Roughly 20 g or more | Steadier energy, fuller for longer |
| Potassium | Often 400 mg or more | Usually less (straining removes some) | Alcohol increases fluid and mineral loss |
| Calcium | High, often a third or more of a day's needs | Moderate to high | General nutrition; not a hangover fix |
| Natural sugar (lactose) | Higher | Lower | Matters if dairy bothers your stomach |
| Water | Mostly water | Less, because it's strained | Small help with fluids |

Two things stand out. First, regular yogurt tends to have more potassium and more fluid, while Greek yogurt has far more protein and less lactose. Second, neither has much sodium, which is the main mineral you need to replace if you're dehydrated. That's why pairing yogurt with a drink that has some salt in it, or a salty side, makes more sense than relying on yogurt alone.

## The Probiotic Angle: Does Yogurt Help Your Gut After Drinking?

This is the main reason people search for yogurt as a hangover food, so it's worth being careful about what is known and what isn't.

### What alcohol does to your gut

Alcohol is hard on the digestive tract. Heavy drinking irritates the stomach lining, speeds up or disrupts how food moves through the intestines (which is why loose stools after drinking are so common), and can make the gut lining temporarily leakier. Research, much of it in people who drink heavily over long periods and in animals, has linked alcohol to changes in the balance of gut bacteria and to bacterial by-products slipping from the gut into the bloodstream, where they can feed inflammation. Our guide to [how alcohol affects your gut microbiome](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-affects-your-gut-microbiome-the-hidden-health-impact-2025) goes into this in more detail.

### What yogurt's cultures can and can't do

Yogurt is made by adding bacteria, usually *Lactobacillus bulgaricus* and *Streptococcus thermophilus*, to milk. Many brands add other strains such as *Lactobacillus acidophilus* or *Bifidobacterium*. Those live cultures are the reason yogurt is often described as a probiotic food.

Here's the honest picture:

- **There is no good evidence that eating yogurt the morning after makes a hangover milder or shorter.** We could not find solid human trials testing yogurt as a hangover treatment.
- **Probiotics need time.** Where probiotics have shown benefits for gut health, it's generally with regular use over days or weeks, not a single serving. One bowl of yogurt is unlikely to reshape your gut bacteria by lunchtime.
- **Lab and animal research is interesting but early.** Some studies have looked at whether certain bacterial strains can break down alcohol or acetaldehyde, or protect the gut lining in animals given alcohol. That work doesn't tell us what a cup of supermarket yogurt does in a person with a hangover.
- **The cultures do help with lactose.** This one is better supported. The live cultures in yogurt help digest the lactose in it, which is why many people who struggle with milk do fine with yogurt. European food regulators have accepted a health claim along these lines for live yogurt cultures.

So the most realistic benefit of the cultures on a hangover morning is that yogurt is easier to digest than a glass of milk, not that it detoxes anything. If you're specifically interested in probiotic products sold for hangovers, such as ZBiotics, which uses a genetically engineered bacterium designed to break down acetaldehyde, we look at the evidence in our [hangover probiotics review](/never-hungover/hangover-probiotics). Those products work on a different idea from ordinary yogurt cultures and should be judged on their own evidence.

### Yogurt for diarrhea after drinking

If drinking leaves you with loose stools the next day, yogurt is a reasonable food choice. It's bland, it's not greasy, and it doesn't contain the spice, fat, or caffeine that can make things worse. Probiotics have some evidence for certain types of diarrhea, such as diarrhea linked to antibiotics, but that research doesn't transfer directly to the kind that follows a night of drinking. Plain yogurt is a sensible thing to eat while your gut settles; it isn't a treatment. Our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) covers what actually helps and when to worry.

## Greek Yogurt vs Regular Yogurt for a Hangover

Both work. The better choice depends on what your stomach and appetite are like.

**Choose Greek yogurt if:**

- Dairy sometimes upsets your stomach. Straining removes much of the whey, which carries a good share of the lactose.
- You want more protein to carry you through a slow morning.
- You can only manage a small amount of food. A few spoonfuls of Greek yogurt deliver more protein than the same amount of regular.

**Choose regular yogurt if:**

- You want something thinner and easier to swallow when you feel nauseated.
- You'd like a bit more potassium and fluid per serving.
- Thick, tangy Greek yogurt feels like too much right now.

**Skip, or go easy on:**

- **Heavily sweetened flavored yogurts.** Some contain as much added sugar as a dessert. A little sweetness is fine, but a big sugar hit on an empty stomach can make you feel shaky later.
- **Yogurt "desserts" and frozen yogurt.** Fine as a treat, but they're mostly sugar and often contain few or no live cultures once frozen and processed. Check the label for "live and active cultures" if that matters to you.
- **Very high-fat yogurts if you're nauseated.** Fat slows stomach emptying, which can make a queasy stomach feel heavier.

## Kefir, Lassi, and Ayran: Drinkable Yogurt for a Hangover

If eating feels impossible, drinking your yogurt can be easier.

- **Kefir** is a fermented milk drink made with a broader mix of bacteria and yeasts than standard yogurt. It's thinner, tangy, and often lower in lactose than milk. Like yogurt, there's no good evidence it treats a hangover, but it's an easy way to get protein and fluid in when you don't want to chew.
- **Salted lassi** (from South Asia) and **ayran** (popular in Turkey and nearby countries) are yogurt mixed with water and salt. That combination is genuinely sensible the morning after: you get fluid, a little sodium, and some protein in one glass. You can make a simple version at home by blending plain yogurt with cold water, a pinch of salt, and ice. Sweet mango lassi is tasty but much higher in sugar.
- **Drinkable yogurts sold in stores** vary a lot. Many are closer to milkshakes in sugar content. Read the label.

If you're mainly worried about fluids, a drink built for rehydration will do more than any yogurt drink. Our guide to [making a homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) shows how to get the salt and sugar balance right.

## Yogurt vs Milk for a Hangover

Yogurt and milk come from the same place, but they sit differently in a hungover stomach.

- **Yogurt is usually easier to digest** because the cultures have already started on the lactose and continue to help break it down.
- **Milk is more fluid** and can feel soothing, but a big glass of cold milk can sit badly if you're nauseated or mildly lactose intolerant.
- **Both offer protein, potassium, and calcium**, and neither is a cure.

We cover milk, chocolate milk, and the "coating your stomach" idea in our page on [milk for a hangover](/never-hungover/milk-for-hangover). If milk generally works for you, either is fine. If milk bloats you, start with yogurt.

## Should You Eat Yogurt Before Drinking?

Eating before you drink is one of the most reliable things you can do to soften the night. Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol passes into your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed, so your blood alcohol rises more slowly and peaks lower. That's well established.

Yogurt can be part of that meal, but on its own it's a light snack, not a lining. A cup of yogurt has some protein and fat but not much bulk. Something more substantial, with protein, fat, and fiber, does a better job: think yogurt with oats and nuts, or a proper dinner with yogurt on the side. Our guide to [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) explains which meals help most.

One note: the idea that yogurt "coats your stomach" and blocks alcohol is a myth. No food forms a protective layer. Food simply slows absorption, and a fuller meal slows it more.

## Can You Eat Yogurt With a Hangover if You're Nauseated?

Often, yes, and it's one of the better choices. A few tips:

1. **Wait until the worst has passed.** If you're actively vomiting, stick to small sips of water or an electrolyte drink first. Try food once you've kept fluids down for an hour or so.
2. **Start small.** A few spoonfuls is enough to test the waters. If it sits well, have more.
3. **Keep it plain and cold.** Cold foods tend to smell less and feel more soothing.
4. **Add a little ginger if you like it.** Grated fresh ginger or a pinch of ground ginger stirred in with honey is a combination many people find settling. Ginger has reasonable evidence for some kinds of nausea; for more, see our page on [ginger for a hangover](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover).
5. **Pair it with something dry.** Plain toast or crackers next to yogurt is a classic, easy-on-the-stomach combination.

For a fuller plan when your stomach is the main problem, our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) walks through what helps and what to avoid.

## How to Build a Better Hangover Yogurt Bowl

Yogurt on its own is fine, but a few additions turn it into a more complete hangover breakfast. Here's a simple formula: **yogurt for protein, a carb for energy, and fluid on the side.**

**Good add-ins:**

- **Banana.** Adds easy carbohydrate and more potassium, and it's soft and mild. See our page on [bananas for a hangover](/never-hungover/bananas-for-hangover) for what bananas can and can't do.
- **Honey.** Quick, gentle sugar if you feel shaky or haven't eaten in a while. A drizzle is enough.
- **Oats or granola.** Slower-burning carbs that help the meal last. Choose a lower-sugar granola, or plain oats.
- **Berries.** Easy to eat, add flavor and fluid, and bring some fiber.
- **A pinch of salt and some cucumber** if you prefer savory, in the style of raita or tzatziki. It sounds odd at breakfast but it adds sodium, which yogurt lacks.

**Three easy combinations:**

1. **The gentle bowl:** plain Greek yogurt, half a sliced banana, a drizzle of honey. Good when you're a little queasy.
2. **The fuller bowl:** regular yogurt, oats, berries, a spoonful of nut butter. Good once your appetite is back.
3. **The savory bowl:** plain yogurt, grated cucumber, a pinch of salt, a little mint, eaten with toast or pita. Good if sweet food doesn't appeal.

If you want something warm and more substantial afterward, eggs are another strong choice. Our page on [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) explains the cysteine idea behind them, and our roundup of the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover) compares the main options side by side.

## What Yogurt Can't Do

It's worth being clear about the limits, because hangover advice online tends to overpromise.

- **It won't sober you up.** Your liver processes alcohol at a fairly fixed pace. No food speeds that up in a meaningful way.
- **It won't rehydrate you on its own.** It helps a little, but you still need to drink fluids, ideally with some sodium.
- **It won't "detox" your liver.** Claims that probiotics or any food "flush out toxins" overnight aren't supported by evidence.
- **It won't fix lost sleep.** Alcohol disrupts the second half of the night's sleep, and a lot of hangover fatigue comes from that. Rest is the only fix.
- **It won't make the next drinking session safer.** A habit of yogurt the morning after doesn't change how alcohol affects your body the night before.

## Who Should Be Careful With Yogurt

Yogurt is safe for most people, but a few groups should think twice:

- **People with a milk allergy.** This is different from lactose intolerance. A true allergy is to milk proteins, and yogurt contains them. Avoid it.
- **People who are very lactose intolerant.** Many tolerate yogurt, and Greek yogurt in particular, but not everyone. Lactose-free yogurt is widely available.
- **People with a weakened immune system.** Live-culture products are safe for almost everyone, but if you've been told to avoid live probiotics because of a medical condition or treatment, follow that advice.
- **Anyone on a medical diet** that limits protein, potassium, or dairy, such as some people with kidney disease. Ask your doctor what fits your plan.

## A Note on Prevention: What Actually Reduces Hangovers

The most effective hangover strategy is unglamorous: drink less, drink more slowly, eat a proper meal beforehand, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, and give yourself time to sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also add a supplement on nights they plan to drink. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research is in animals and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers outright. If you want to try it, a straightforward, budget-friendly option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts. None of this replaces drinking sensibly, eating well, and staying hydrated.

## The Bottom Line

- Yogurt is one of the gentlest, most practical foods to eat with a hangover: cool, soft, high in protein, and low in sugar if you choose plain.
- It provides protein, potassium, calcium, and a little fluid, but very little sodium, so pair it with water or an electrolyte drink and maybe something salty.
- There is no good evidence that yogurt's probiotic cultures make a hangover milder or shorter. The best-supported benefit of the cultures is easier lactose digestion.
- Greek yogurt suits people who are sensitive to dairy or want more protein; regular yogurt is thinner and has a bit more potassium and fluid.
- Salted yogurt drinks such as ayran or lassi combine fluid, salt, and protein, which makes them a sensible choice the morning after.
- If you can't keep fluids down, have severe belly pain, see blood, or feel confused, get medical help rather than trying another food.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is yogurt good for a hangover?**

Yogurt is a good food to eat with a hangover because it's easy on an upset stomach and provides protein, potassium, calcium, and a little fluid. Plain yogurt is also low in added sugar. It doesn't cure a hangover, clear alcohol faster, or rehydrate you on its own, so pair it with water or an electrolyte drink and give yourself time to recover.

**Do the probiotics in yogurt help with a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that the live cultures in yogurt make a hangover milder or shorter. Where probiotics show benefits for gut health, it's generally with regular use over days or weeks, not a single serving. The best-supported benefit of yogurt's cultures is that they help digest lactose, which makes yogurt easier on the stomach than milk for many people.

**Is Greek yogurt or regular yogurt better for a hangover?**

Both work. Greek yogurt has much more protein and less lactose, which helps if dairy sometimes bothers your stomach. Regular yogurt is thinner, easier to swallow when you're nauseated, and usually has a bit more potassium and fluid. Choose plain versions of either and add your own banana or honey rather than buying heavily sweetened flavors.

**Is it good to eat yogurt before drinking alcohol?**

Eating before drinking slows how fast alcohol is absorbed, and yogurt can be part of that. On its own, though, a cup of yogurt is a light snack. A fuller meal with protein, fat, and fiber slows absorption more. Yogurt doesn't coat your stomach or block alcohol; that idea is a myth.

**Can yogurt help with diarrhea after drinking?**

Plain yogurt is a reasonable, bland food to eat while your gut settles after drinking, since it isn't greasy, spicy, or caffeinated. Probiotics have some evidence for certain types of diarrhea, such as diarrhea linked to antibiotics, but that doesn't directly apply to diarrhea after alcohol. See a doctor if it lasts more than a couple of days, contains blood, or comes with severe pain or signs of dehydration.

**Is kefir better than yogurt for a hangover?**

Kefir is drinkable, contains a wider range of bacteria and yeasts, and is often lower in lactose than milk, so it can be easier to get down when you don't feel like eating. There is no good evidence that it treats a hangover better than yogurt. Choose whichever you can tolerate, and drink water or an electrolyte drink alongside it.

**What should I put in yogurt for a hangover?**

A simple, effective bowl pairs yogurt with an easy carbohydrate: sliced banana, a drizzle of honey, oats, or berries. If you're nauseated, a little ginger and honey stirred in can help. If you prefer savory, plain yogurt with cucumber, a pinch of salt, and mint adds some sodium, which yogurt otherwise lacks.
